title: Mata Jito
hookLine: Guru Gobind Singh's wife, whom tradition credits with the sugar in the first amrit

lines: AN IRON BOWL, A DOUBLE-EDGED BLADE.
cards: An iron bowl. Clear water. A double-edged blade turning slowly through it, while hymns are recited over it, verse after verse.
This is the scene Sikhs tell from the day the Khalsa was born at Anandpur: the Guru preparing amrit, the water of initiation. It's a scene of steel.
Then, in the telling, someone steps forward with something small in her hands: sugar, little puffed sweets. She doesn't make a speech. She just drops them into the bowl.
And the story says the Guru let them stay. Today: Mata Jito.

teach.h: A WIFE OF GURU GOBIND SINGH.
teach.b: Mata Jito was a wife of Guru Gobind Singh. Mata means mother, a title of honor Sikhs use for the women of the Guru's household.
Tradition remembers her as the mother of several of the Guru's sons, the ones Sikhs call the Sahibzade. Now, the bowl.
Amrit is made with water and sugar puffs called patashas, stirred with a khanda, a double-edged sword, while sacred compositions are recited.
The sugar is part of it to this day, and the story of how it got there is a story about a woman. The Guru was stirring the steel through the water. A wife of the Guru came and added the sweets.
One telling says the Guru took it as a sign: the Khalsa would be brave, and it would also be sweet. Here the sources differ, and it's worth saying plainly.
Some tellings, including the one this path follows today, give the sweets to Mata Jito. Others give the same moment to Mata Sahib Kaur, whom we meet in two days.
Sikhs hold both tellings, and nobody needs to settle it to see the point. Steel alone can make someone hard. A sword can protect, but it can also make a person proud, quick, cold.

teach.h: COURAGE AND GENTLENESS IN ONE BOWL.
teach.b: The story puts sweetness in the same bowl, so whoever drinks it is meant to carry both: courage and gentleness, a straight back and a soft word.
Sikhs speak of the ideal as saint and soldier together. This little story shows the saint half being stirred in, by a woman's hand, at the very bowl where the Khalsa began.

how: At an amrit ceremony, the Panj Pyare prepare amrit from water and patashas in an iron bowl, stirring it with a khanda while reciting set compositions, and Sikhs tell the story of the sweets being added by a wife of the Guru.

o: a woman who led the Sikhs by letter after the Guru died
the Guru's mother, who kept his sons steady in the tower
a wife of Guru Gobind Singh, linked to the sweets in amrit

games.q: you're the Guru, stirring steel through water for the first amrit. a woman of your house quietly drops sweets into the bowl. what do you do?
o: stop and start again with clean water.
let them stay, and take it as a sign.
ask her to leave the ceremony.
games.why: in the telling, the Guru let the sweets stay: the Khalsa would be brave, and sweet too. sugar is in amrit to this day.

practice: Think of one place where you have to be strong right now: a hard conversation, a decision, someone you have to stand up to.
Keep the strength, and picture sweetness in the same moment, a kinder first sentence, a pause before answering, a thank-you you'd usually skip. Hold both in the same bowl for a few breaths.
